{"id": "18:11/q07", "question": "What do reports say happened as the youths entered the cave?", "turns_on": "Accounts vary in when sleep began and in surrounding details.", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q07/p1", "position": "God put them to sleep in the cave, with the dog and their provisions beside them.", "reasons": "Tabari places sleep after their meal and conversation, with the dog at the entrance. Tha'labi puts it at sunset, provisions by their heads. A report from Abu Abd Allah says they entered with the dog, slept until the king and city disappeared, then awoke thinking a day or part of one had passed. Tabataba'i summarizes the protected cave sleep."}, {"id": "18:11/q07/p2", "position": "They slept as soon as they entered the cave, hiding them from the kingdom.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports this chronology."}, {"id": "18:11/q07/p3", "position": "The youths fled an idol worshipping tyrant with a shepherd and his dog.", "reasons": "Abu Abd Allah's report has the tyrant kill dissenters; the youths feigned a hunting trip and the shepherd joined their faith. Tha'labi adds that Tamlikha warned them of Daqyanus, after which they prostrated and sought protection; the king later could not find them and leaders accused them of rebellion."}]}

{"id": "18:11/q09", "question": "Where was the cave thought to be?", "turns_on": "Whether archaeology and geography can identify a proposed cave.", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q09/p1", "position": "Rujayb in Jordan is the strongest proposed fit, though no cave is conclusively identified.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i favors the excavated Rujayb site for its signs and some Muslim reports, while also saying none is proved. {"id": "18:11/q10", "question": "Were the youths alive during their long sleep?", "turns_on": "Whether the condition is ordinary sleep, a sleep-like death, or an intermediate state.", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q10/p1", "position": "They remained alive, asleep, and protected; they had not died.", "reasons": "Mawardi says the stopped hearing indicates sleep rather than death. {"id": "18:11/q11", "question": "How long did they sleep?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes state only a counted span or identify it with 309 years in 18:25.", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q11/p1", "position": "The stay lasted 309 years.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Mujahid give 309; Razi calls it 309 years of protected sleep. {"id": "18:11/q13", "question": "How is 'ʿadadan' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether it modifies 'years' as an adjective or verbal noun, or acts as an independent cognate accusative.", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q13/p1", "position": "It modifies 'years' as counted or possessing a number.", "reasons": "Farra, Zajjaj, Tha'labi, Wahidi, Razi, Ibn Jawzi, Qurtubi, and Samin give the adjectival analysis. {"id": "18:11/q14", "question": "What does calling the years 'counted' imply?", "turns_on": "Whether explicit counting evokes abundance, brevity, either scale, complete years, or an unspecified length.", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q14/p1", "position": "It suggests many years, since a small quantity needs no counting.", "reasons": "Zajjaj states the principle; Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Jawzi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Biqa'i, and Tabataba'i's report of Zajjaj repeat it. Alusi says it suits the same point, and al-Kashf links it to a singular addressee. Abu Hayyan rejects comparison with 23:113, which concerns the sight of promised punishment. Bagawi reports that counting may simply emphasize number or a long period."}]}

{"id": "18:11/q18", "question": "What can be learned from the varying historical accounts of the cave story?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q18/p1", "position": "Reports diverge greatly; the Qur'an selects what serves guidance and omits many historical particulars.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i lists disagreement over dates, kings, lineage, looks, names, and the title People of the Inscription. {"id": "18:11/q19", "question": "How does Ibn Qutayba approach the figurative wording of this verse amid criticism of Qur'anic style?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q19/p1", "position": "He explains its metaphor through tafsir, Arab language, and possible readings while resisting unsupported personal interpretation and later charges against Qur'anic style.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says literal translation of the ear expression obscures its sense. {"id": "18:11/q20", "question": "What verbal features does al-Baqillani identify in Qur'anic eloquence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q20/p1", "position": "Its expression has harmonious letters, meaning-led verse endings, and related word forms; its sound, clear meaning, and proof affect discerning listeners.", "reasons": "Al-Baqillani defines tala'um as fitting letter arrangement and contrasts it with the harsh 'grave of Harb' tongue-twister; he places poetry's harmony below the Qur'an's highest grade, while noting variation among listeners. He reports al-Khalil's account of dissonance from articulation points too near or too far apart. He distinguishes Qur'anic fawasil, whose identical or neighboring end letters follow meaning, from saj' and the tighter constraints of poetic rhyme and meter. He also introduces tajanis for forms sharing a root."}]}
{"id": "18:11/q21", "question": "May the Arabic wording of this verse be recited in translation?", "turns_on": "Whether recitation requires the Arabic form tied to the Qur'an's inimitability, and whether inability to read Arabic permits Persian.", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q21/p1", "position": "No; recitation must retain its Arabic form, in and out of prayer, even for someone unable to read Arabic.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan holds that the Qur'an's inimitability is bound to its Arabic form and reports consensus on retaining that form: translation loses expressive precision, and even Arabic paraphrase cannot replace the challenged wording. {"id": "18:11/q22", "question": "What does the divine plural in فَضَرَبْنَا convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:11/q22/p1", "position": "It conveys divine majesty and abundance; a following singular indication prevents reading the plural as multiple gods.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai says the divine plural appears in contexts of greatness and abundance, while singular forms occur elsewhere, citing 94:1 and 74:11. {"id": "18:16/q04", "question": "What prompted the youths' withdrawal and how did they leave?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over prior concealment, public confession, and whether the youths coordinated before leaving or recognized each other only in the wilderness.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q04/p1", "position": "They fled persecution and forced idolatry, acting together or resolving to leave together.", "reasons": "Thalabi says they feared Daqyanus and took provisions; Ibn Abbas says seven fled by night after an idol-worship summons. Tabatabai prefers a public confession at an enforcing assembly, citing a report that six were royal advisers, yet allows earlier concealed belief. Islahi sees imminent stoning and a chosen cave."}, {"id": "18:16/q04/p2", "position": "They left separately, unaware of one another's faith, and pledged common belief when they met outside the city.", "reasons": "Reports of al-Sadiq and Ibn Abbas, cited by Tabatabai, describe separate departures and cautious exchange in the wilderness; Ibn Abbas says God brought them together unexpectedly. {"id": "18:16/q06", "question": "What happened as they settled in the cave and after they disappeared?", "turns_on": "Reports disagree whether the fugitives remained hidden, were sealed in, or met the king; Ibn Kathir tests the sealing story against the sunlight of 18:17.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q06/p1", "position": "They lived there briefly with provisions, then God put them to sleep.", "reasons": "Thalabi says they took remaining supplies; Ibn Abbas says they prayed and praised God while Tamlikha secretly bought food, disguised in poor clothes, and checked news. Kuran Yolu says God accepted their plea through a long sleep; Elmalili links sleep to 18:10–11 and protection from distress."}, {"id": "18:16/q06/p2", "position": "The ruler searched but could not find them.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares their concealment to the Prophet and Abu Bakr in Thawr and cites 9:40. {"id": "18:16/q08", "question": "How does 'what they worship' relate grammatically to 'you withdrew from them'?", "turns_on": "Whether mā names objects, makes worship a verbal noun, or negates a parenthetical clause.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q08/p1", "position": "Mā is a relative pronoun in the accusative, coordinated with the object pronoun: they left the people and their worshipped objects.", "reasons": "Tabari, Zajjaj, Kashshaf, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Atiyya as cited by Qurtubi, and Samin explain coordination; Samin notes an omitted object in the relative clause and that the exception can attach to mā or its object pronoun. Burhan includes this mā among relative mā clauses, alongside what is harvested, prepared, or married."}, {"id": "18:16/q08/p2", "position": "Mā is infinitival: they left the people's worship, with an implied 'worship' supplying the exception.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Samin, Bursevi, and Alusi give this alternative; Alusi requires the omitted act of worship for a connected exception. Samin says the two possibilities for the exception remain."}, {"id": "18:16/q08/p3", "position": "Mā is negative, making a parenthetical declaration that the youths worship none but God.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Samin, Abu Hayyan, Baydawi, Nasafi, Kashshaf, and Alusi give this divine parenthesis; illā is an unrestricted exception. Alusi says al-Kashf relates it to the following clause. Samin criticizes Abu al-Baqa for wrongly tying connected and disconnected exceptions solely to the negative analysis. Itqan also classifies mā before illā here under the general negative reading."}]}
{"id": "18:16/q09", "question": "What does 'except God' imply about the people's worship?", "turns_on": "Whether the idolaters also worshipped God; Tabatabai and Alusi cite the surrounding passage against that inference.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q09/p1", "position": "The exception is connected: the people acknowledged or worshipped God alongside idols, and the youths abandoned only the idols.", "reasons": "Muqatil says they retain knowledge of their Lord and Creator. Baghawi explicitly says the common reading implies worship of God and idols. Ata al-Khurasani and Farra report such shared worship; Kashshaf compares Meccans. Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, Bursevi, and Alusi make this conditional on the people's practice."}, {"id": "18:16/q09/p2", "position": "The exception is disconnected: the people worshipped only idols, so God was never among the objects abandoned.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Kashshaf, Nasafi, Samin, Bursevi, and Alusi allow this conditional reading. Alusi says it better fits 18:15. Tabatabai prefers it because the passage gives no sign the idolaters worshipped God too."}, {"id": "18:16/q09/p3", "position": "The phrase means 'other than God': they gave up every worshipped object apart from Him, without deciding whether the townspeople worshipped Him.", "reasons": "Qatada's reading is treated this way by Ibn Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya as quoted by Qurtubi; Ibn Masud's explanatory wording makes it explicit."}, {"id": "18:16/q09/p4", "position": "Their people's coerced submission to God's will and decrees can itself be called worship.", "reasons": "Biqai offers this as a possible account of the wording."}]}
{"id": "18:16/q10", "question": "What alternate wording is transmitted for 'what they worship except God'?", "turns_on": "The wording of codex reports; Abu Hayyan judges both against the universally transmitted consonantal text.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q10/p1", "position": "Ibn Masud's codex says 'what they worship besides God.'", "reasons": "Qatada or Ibn Masud is cited across Yahya, Tabari, Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Durr, and Alusi. Abu Hayyan and Alusi's citation of al-Bahr say it is an explanatory gloss rather than Qurʾān because it conflicts with the transmitted consonantal text. Burhan says added or omitted wording is recited only if supported by regional Uthmani codices and introducing no unasserted ruling; a Companion reading can still provide stronger interpretive evidence than ordinary tafsir."}, {"id": "18:16/q10/p2", "position": "Some copies instead say 'what they worship besides us.'", "reasons": "Harun reports this Ibn Masud codex variant; Abu Hayyan quotes it, and Alusi also records it. It too is described as an explanatory gloss rather than a canonical reading. Burhan's general rule requires codex support for recitation of differing wording, while treating Companion readings as strong evidence for interpretation."}]}
{"id": "18:16/q11", "question": "What is the grammatical role of 'when you withdrew' relative to 'take refuge'?", "turns_on": "Whether idh can carry a conditional force, or is temporal or causal with an explicit or omitted governor.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q11/p1", "position": "The cave command is the response to 'when,' treated like a conditional: when you withdraw, take refuge.", "reasons": "Farra is cited by Wahidi, Razi, Bursevi, and Alusi. Nahhas says the command in turn has 'your Lord will spread' as its answer. {"id": "18:16/q14", "question": "What mercy is promised to them?", "turns_on": "Whether the benefits stressed are worldly sustenance and safety, broader divine care, or spiritual provision.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q14/p1", "position": "God will expand provision and protective care, including their sleep and relief from danger.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls their sleep the provision. {"id": "18:16/q15", "question": "Why could they speak so confidently of God's help?", "turns_on": "Whether certainty is explained by faith, prior prophetic knowledge, or God's direct promise; Alusi rejects prophetic speculation and Islahi rejects a human assurance.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q15/p1", "position": "Their trust, hope, and certainty in God gave them confidence.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Nasafi, Baydawi, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi, and Tabatabai connect the assurance with trust. {"id": "18:16/q16", "question": "What does 'He will prepare' imply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q16/p1", "position": "God will arrange and make easy what benefits them.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas in Abu Hayyan says the king's threats become easy to bear with kindness and comfort; Alusi glosses yuhayyiʾ as making easy and takes its omitted object as good or like benefit."}]}
{"id": "18:16/q17", "question": "How does 'from your affair' attach, and what does 'from' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether min expresses source, part, or replacement, and whether the phrase attaches to the verb or to marfiqan.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q17/p1", "position": "It attaches to 'prepare'; min marks source or a portion of their affair.", "reasons": "Samin gives both source and partitive possibilities, repeated by Alusi."}, {"id": "18:16/q17/p2", "position": "Min means 'instead of': God prepares relief in place of their difficult situation.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari cites a poem wishing for Zamzam in place of another water; Abu Hayyan notes the same line, and Alusi also invokes 9:38. {"id": "18:16/q18", "question": "What does mirfaq mean in this promise?", "turns_on": "Whether the general useful comfort is specified as food, escape, or replacement of hardship.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q18/p1", "position": "A useful means of comfort, ease, support, or beneficial accommodation.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda, Akhfash, Tabari, Thalabi, and many later authors define practical support; Tabari ties it to distress and fear for life and faith. Mawrdi also offers spacious relief, and Tabatabai gentle treatment. Islahi calls it anything useful, Asad concrete or abstract benefit. Lexicographers also use it for the elbow, the bodily support joint."}, {"id": "18:16/q18/p2", "position": "Specifically food or provisions, even breakfast.", "reasons": "Kalbi in Wahidi glosses breakfast, Suddi in Durr says food; Wahidi Wajiz says an easy source of food and Thalabi describes a comfortable provision. Damghani takes mirfaq as provision in the youths' request for practical help."}, {"id": "18:16/q18/p3", "position": "A way out, rescue, or deliverance.", "reasons": "Mawardi offers rescue; Wahidi reports others' gloss as an exit."}, {"id": "18:16/q18/p4", "position": "A replacement of their hardship with a better situation.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari is cited by Ibn Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, with a poetic use of substitute."}]}
{"id": "18:16/q19", "question": "How is mirfaq read?", "turns_on": "Regional and transmitted vocalization; sources disagree on some individual reader attributions, but Tabari accepts both main forms.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q19/p1", "position": "Kasra on mīm and fatḥa on fāʾ: mirfaq.", "reasons": "Five canonical readers Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Asim, Hamza and Kisai are repeatedly listed; Ibn Atiyya adds Hasan, Talha, Aʿmash, and Ibn Abi Ishaq. Tabari prefers this Iraqi form as common and eloquent, while accepting both. Farra says Aʿmash and Hasan use it; Abu Hayyan and Razi give transmission variants for Abu Amr or Asim. Ibn al-Jazari assigns the kasra-on-mīm, fatḥa-on-fāʾ form to all readers other than the two Medinese readers and Ibn ʿAmir."}, {"id": "18:16/q19/p2", "position": "Fatḥa on mīm and kasra on fāʾ: marfiq.", "reasons": "Nafi and Ibn Amir, with Medina and Syria, recur in the lists; Farra also names Medina's readers and Asim, Baghawi adds Abu Jaʿfar, and Abu Hayyan and Alusi list Abu Jaʿfar, Aʿraj, Shayba, Humayd, Ibn Saʿdan and one Abu Amr report. Ibn Mujahid and Farisi report an Abu Bakr or Kisai transmission; Baydawi calls the form an anomalous verbal noun. Ibn al-Jazari assigns the open-mīm, kasra-on-fāʾ form to both Medinese readers and Ibn ʿAmir."}, {"id": "18:16/q19/p3", "position": "Both mīm and fāʾ may be open.", "reasons": "Muʿadh permits this as a verbal noun in Abu Hayyan and Samin; Alusi also records it."}]}
{"id": "18:16/q20", "question": "Do the mirfaq forms differ in sense or formation?", "turns_on": "Whether the vocalizations are equivalent dialects or mark different nouns; reports conflict even about Kisai's and Farra's usage.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q20/p1", "position": "Both are dialect forms usable for a helpful thing and, in many accounts, an elbow.", "reasons": "Farra cites a rajaz pairing the forms; Zajjaj, Qutrub, Abu al-Hasan, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, and Alusi allow both. Akhfash and Abu al-Hasan explain a noun like masjid, a dialect form, or rifq; Razi says derived from irtifāq. Farra says most Arabs prefer kasra for both, though some use fatḥa. Samin disputes a report that Farra knew only kasra by citing the transmitted Nafi and Syrian readings."}, {"id": "18:16/q20/p2", "position": "The vowels distinguish the aid or facility from the body's elbow, though sources assign them differently.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh, Abu Ubayda, Yunus, Farra on Hijaz speech, and Ibn Jawzi associate kasra with the elbow or comfort in differing ways; Kisai is quoted both as accepting only kasra for elbow (Tabari/Razi) and only open mīm (Abu Hayyan/Samin/Alusi). Abu Hatim makes the open form a place noun, Abu Zayd a verbal noun. Mawrdi distinguishes received benefit from benefit extended; Qiraat-ER notes instrumental, locative, or nominal patterns."}, {"id": "18:16/q20/p3", "position": "Only the kasra-on-mīm form is known or fluent across senses.", "reasons": "Asmaʿi says he knows only kasra; Nahhas reports him across matter, hand, and all senses. Farra is reported similarly by Abu Hayyan and Alusi, though other Farra reports allow both. Nahhas calls kasra the fluent form; Samin objects that Nafi and Syrian transmission proves open mīm exists."}]}

{"id": "18:16/q23", "question": "What inward meaning is given to leaving the people and entering the cave?", "turns_on": "Whether the cave signifies solitary devotion, bodily discipline, or the path of divine union.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q23/p1", "position": "Leave everything besides God, including bad company and desires, and retreat into solitude with Him.", "reasons": "Qushayri says detachment yields union and divine shelter; Bursevi cites al-Hujandi's line that union follows severance. {"id": "18:16/q27", "question": "How does the Qurʾanic account relate to later historical reports?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q27/p1", "position": "The reports vary widely, while the Qurʾān selects details needed for guidance.", "reasons": "Tabatabai lists differences over disclosure to the ruler, joint plans, shepherd and dog, discovery and death, dates, rulers, lineage, names, sleepers' number and duration. {"id": "18:16/q29", "question": "What other report concerns the youths' age or status?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q29/p1", "position": "The youths illustrate that prophets were sent and scholars received learning while young.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas is cited by Alusi, with Abraham, Moses, and the cave youths as examples from 21:60, 18:60, and 18:13."}]}
{"id": "18:16/q30", "question": "Why is the name Muʿtazila connected with withdrawal?", "turns_on": "Which historical act of separation gave the group its name.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q30/p1", "position": "The name refers to leaving al-Hasan's circle, associated with ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd.", "reasons": "Jishumi says it followed al-Hasan's death; Tabrisi relates it to ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd's circle leaving al-Hasan's gathering."}, {"id": "18:16/q30/p2", "position": "The name means rejecting innovations and following the early community.", "reasons": "Jishumi records this alternative derivation."}]}

{"id": "18:16/q32", "question": "How is the hamza in yuhayyiʾ written in the codices?", "turns_on": "Whether the Syrian codex attests an alif spelling despite al-Dani's claimed consensus.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q32/p1", "position": "An alif writes the hamza in some codices, including the Syrian codex.", "reasons": "Al-Ghazi ibn Qays reports this spelling to avoid excessive deletion after a doubled yāʾ. {"id": "18:16/q33", "question": "What pause treatments are given for the hamza in and around yuhayyiʾ?", "turns_on": "The hamza's written seat, preceding letter, vowel, and whether its sukun is obligatory.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q33/p1", "position": "The written seat governs the pause: wāw or yāʾ permits eased rūm, while alif calls for substitution.", "reasons": "Some readers distinguish these cases, and Makki and Ibn Shurayḥ choose the distinction."}, {"id": "18:16/q33/p2", "position": "Eased rūm applies after an alif, but not after a moving letter.", "reasons": "Ibn Balima draws this restriction."}, {"id": "18:16/q33/p3", "position": "Eased rūm extends through the three hamza vowels, with two options after a moving letter for ḍamma and kasra.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Faḥḥām gives these options; Ibn Sawwar agrees for hamza after alif."}, {"id": "18:16/q33/p4", "position": "Eased rūm is allowed for every hamza vowel after either alif or another letter, even with fatḥa.", "reasons": "Some give this exceptional option; al-Dani records it without claiming to have received it, and Ibn Ghalbun records but disapproves of it."}, {"id": "18:16/q33/p5", "position": "At pause, a necessarily silent hamza is replaced by a long-vowel letter that jussive syntax cannot remove.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari applies this to yuhayyiʾ and rejects both full hamza articulation and deletion of the substitute at pause."}, {"id": "18:16/q33/p6", "position": "For a ḍamma hamza after kasra, five transmitted pause faces include yāʾ substitution, rūm or ishām, and two eased articulations.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari lists these for yunsʾi and similar forms, attributing one yāʾ form to al-Akhfash and a wāw-like easing on rūm to Sibawayh."}]}

{"id": "18:16/q35", "question": "How is rāʾ thickened or thinned in mirfaq and related recitation rules?", "turns_on": "Whether mīm's kasra is necessary or incidental, and whether tafkhīm is the default for rāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q35/p1", "position": "The rāʾ of mirfaq is thinned because the preceding mīm's kasra is necessary.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari prefers tarqīq even though mīm is an added letter, since removing it damages the word; he compares Warsh's al-miḥrāb and ikhrājan."}, {"id": "18:16/q35/p2", "position": "The rāʾ of mirfaq is thickened because the added mīm's kasra is incidental.", "reasons": "Some authorities thicken it on this analysis; another view calls every kasra on an added letter incidental."}, {"id": "18:16/q35/p3", "position": "In general, tafkhīm is the rāʾ's default and tarqīq needs a cause; rāʾ after ḍamma or before an istiʿlāʾ letter stays thick.", "reasons": "The readers agree on those thickening cases, rejecting a contrary attribution to Warsh; the majority and Makki treat thinning as the restricted case."}, {"id": "18:16/q35/p4", "position": "Rāʾ is neutral between thick and thin, its vowel influence being especially strong.", "reasons": "Other authorities cite the tongue's position near the upper palate and rāʾ's repeated articulation."}]}
{"id": "18:16/q36", "question": "Why is the cave referred to as definite?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:16/q36/p1", "position": "The cave is treated as mentally familiar to the addressee.", "reasons": "Burhan explains that a definite noun can refer to something mentally familiar to its addressee; he compares the cave with the pledge tree in 48:18."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q01", "question": "What does 'thus' compare the awakening with?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative recalls the preceding sleep or heightens the new event.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q01/p1", "position": "God's preceding sleep and preservation of the youths, equally wondrous signs of His power.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi links sleep, increased guidance and turning (18:11,13,18); al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari compare the sleep; al-Baghawi and al-Tabrisi stress preservation from decay; Abu Hayyan sees the earlier compressed account; Alusi says both display overwhelming power."}, {"id": "18:19/q01/p2", "position": "The awakening is likened to itself to magnify its wonder.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares the rhetorical usage at 2:143. {"id": "18:19/q02", "question": "What does 'We raised them' mean and how were they raised?", "turns_on": "Whether baʿth is read as bodily awakening in the account or as an inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q02/p1", "position": "God woke or revived them from a deathlike long sleep, with their bodies and condition preserved.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda relates baʿth to resurrection; Ibn Qutayba and al-Wahidi compare slumber to death; Jishumi gives its root as stirring and its other uses as sending messengers or raising the dead; al-Qurtubi cites a poet's waking usage. Al-Damghānī gives sending a messenger or dispatching someone as another sense of baʿth, citing 62:2 and 2:129."}, {"id": "18:19/q02/p2", "position": "The awakening is an inward return to wakefulness or sobriety.", "reasons": "Qashani calls it the Sufi first awakening, in which faculties discuss latent meanings; Alusi reports the return from spiritual intoxication."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q03", "question": "Why were they awakened to question one another?", "turns_on": "Whether the lām marks a direct purpose or a consequence, and which wisdom the dialogue serves.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q03/p1", "position": "Their questioning was a purpose of the awakening, revealing God's power and the duration's mystery.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Jishumi take the stated end directly; al-Razi says disclosure of divine power is desirable itself; al-Samin prefers causal purpose; Tabatabai ties it to 18:12 and rejects reducing it to a minor consequence; Ibn Ashur says it benefits the youths by direct knowledge of resurrection, like Abraham in 2:260. Al-Biqai adds faith and certainty; al-Tabrisi adds recognition of the Creator and gratitude."}, {"id": "18:19/q03/p2", "position": "Questioning was the resulting event, while the awakening chiefly displayed divine power.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi read the lām as consequence, citing 28:8; al-Baghawi calls questioning an outcome; al-Khafaji prefers this because divine power is the purpose; Asad renders it 'and they began to ask.'
